speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege and to correct, under the rules of the house, a report regarding two replies by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to two questions I asked and placed on the order paper.- I wish to call Your Honour's attention to the fact that the privileges of a member have been taken away by the answers given by the minister. In the first question I complained of a large public meeting held in Quebec city on April 6 and reported at length in the three newspapers of that city, L'Evenement and Le Soleil and another, in which the speaker referred to in the question, Reverend Father Gravel, said:
There must be a revolution. There is no good saying it can't happen here... .1 am for revolution. I will support a revolution that will fight for the independence of this province. Our people must unite and retake the soil which belongs to us.
A lengthy report appeared in L'Evenement of April 6. Practically the same report appears in Le Soleil of the 6th:
When a nation is as sick as this, there is only
one way to save it, revolution___That is the
only remedy which will save us.
Other papers, fifteen in all, had lengthy reports along the same lines, and more details.
Under standing order No. 44, material facts may be cited in order to make a question intelligible. The rule then goes on to refer to the privileges of members; it refers to misquotations. In my question I simply drew attention to a report of a large public meeting in Quebec, and in order to make the question
24S2
Privilege-Mr. Church

intelligible I referred to certain facts-the reports of the meeting. I submit that I was quite within the rules of the house. I did not seek to supply any information to the house but simply to ask a question based on the reports of a meeting which became an unlawful assembly, and therefore the question as I worded it was, I submit, in order. My other question was based on a long report in the Toronto Star Weekly of Saturday, April 23, in a dispatch from Montreal and quoting L'Autorite, in which a scheme to seize Rideau Hall, Ottawa, and the public buildings here was set out at length under a heading Fascist Scheme to Seize Ottawa by Force. These matters I complained of were in many other papers including all our leading Canadian dailies.
Under the rules I was prevented from reading a verbatim report of what the reverend gentleman said. I waited for the government or for some responsible minister to raise this question of public importance and get the real facts and to take action, but nothing was done.
At page 2431 the minister is reported as having made this answer to the first question I asked:
This question serves to show the soundness of the rules of the house to the effect that a question should seek to obtain information, not to supply it to the house.
I repeat, my question did not supply information, but I sought government action; for the information is contained in a two-column verbatim report published in many newspapers. I supplied no answer, only a reference to lengthy press reports. The minister went on to say:
The government is not aware of the facts mentioned by the hon. gentleman-
The occurrences and the meeting to which I have reference in the question were in the minister's own constituency or city and were reported in his own city press. He continued:
-but I know personally that he has been wrongly informed, at least in some important particulars.
I did not make the statement myself which I quoted in the question I asked; it appeared in three newspapers published in Quebec and in others throughout Canada. The mere fact that the minister says that my fears are groundless does not make it so. I simply stated the facts, and as a further question of privilege, I object to untruthful comments in this morning's Citizen and reflections on me. It is in the public interest that in times like

these the government should find out what address this gentleman did make, and examine the press reports and comments, and decide whether any action will be taken in the matter under the law. Section 98 was repealed, but other sections of the code are there with regard to unlawful assemblies and threats of force and revolution.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. A. MacG. YOUNG (Saskatoon): I desire to ask the government a question based upon a report which appeared in the Ottawa Evening Citizen of Monday, May 2, of an address by the premier of Ontario before the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations. I quote:
"And now may I express a long, deep note of discontent," the premier continued, stating the first notice he received of the appointment of the commission, " came at the breakfast table, from a morning newspaper"....
He suggested the objective of the commission bore so directly on the affairs of provincial government that all provinces should have been consulted about the commission appointment. "And I suspect several of the provinces were consulted," he said.
My question is: were some of the provinces consulted regarding the appointment of the Rowell commission?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUESTION AS TO CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES REGARDING APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
I may say to my hon. friend that as far as I am able to recall none

Relief and Agricultural Distress
of the provinces were consulted as to the intention of the government to appoint the commission. The decision of the government was reached by itself after careful consideration of the whole matter and announcement regarding the intention of the government to appoint the commission was made in this house, if I remember rightly, in the middle of February. The commission itself was not appointed until August. The personnel of the commission was made known at that time. In the interval representations were made to the government from many sources as to persons who might be considered and these representations were considered. I cannot say at the moment just what these various representations were, but I would say that no single province was treated differently from any other. All were treated exactly alike. I speak subject to correction, but my recollection is that representations were made by a member of the government of Ontario as to a person who might be appointed to the commission, and the name of that person was considered along with other names which were submitted. The Hon. Mr. Rowell was subsequently appointed from Ontario.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, May 2, consideration in committee of Bill No. 105, to assist in the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress-Mr. Rogers-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 3-Undertaking of measures:

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
It has seemed to me that
in the last week or two a great many speeches have been made that would not have been made if the speakers had more sense of responsibility. We in opposition have no responsibility but to criticize, or possibly offer suggestions. I had no idea of speaking on this bill, but perhaps because I am a woman and have had children I have received letters from women from one end of Canada to the other saying to me: "School days are ending; my boy is coming out of school, what am I to do with him? I have two daughters leaving school; what faces those girls? You as a woman should be able to tell me."
This is quite a responsibility to put on my shoulders, because I do not know what to do with other people's children. As I have watched the minister and listened to the criticisms showered upon him I felt that if attrition could wear a man down he would not be in the house to-day. I do not know that I have ever seen anyone look more exhausted than did the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) when I spoke to him last night. He was tired, he was worn out. I have enough faith in him to believe that he is honestly and conscientiously trying to do his best.
I have watched from the gallery since 1921 government after government: I have heard the same questions asked by the various oppositions: What are you going to do? Why don't you tell us when you bring down your bills what you are going to do? No government I have ever heard of has taken the general public into its confidence until it has fully made its plans; therefore I should not expect the Minister of Labour to take us into his full confidence at the present stage. But when he is employing men to spend the amount of money that is to be voted to him -and it certainly will be voted to him by practically all hon. members of the house, whether they approve of his policy or not- I suggest that he be very careful to place the spending of that money in the hands of men who know how to deal with it. It is easy enough to give to a political supporter the spending of enormous sums of money; and I understand as well as anyone that to the victors belong the spoils. But surely among the ranks of any party there are good men, conscientious men, who in spite of their affiliations with the party in power will do what is right and what is best for the general public.
I want our boys and our girls to have a chance. In the city of Vancouver there are two women well known there who in their
Relief and Agricultural Distress

own way, small though the scope may be compared with the thousands that are out of employment, have done wonders towards helping the young people of that city. One of them is Judge Helen G. MacGill. Speaking from this side of the house, I am sorry that I must say she is a Liberal. She has been for a long time the judge of the juvenile court there. With the help of friends she organized the training of girls for housework. Each year she has exhibitions. The shopkeepers there have helped her place these girls as best they could. Mrs. MacGill organized and has done that work herself. She drew her friends of all shades of politics with her, and has done a wonderful work. The other woman-I know that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) knows her-is Mrs. McKay. She organized the Arts and Crafts Association-although I believe that is not the correct name-but she has brought from all over British Columbia men and women who were immigrants or are the children of immigrants, into an organization in which they have done the work in which they or their parents were skilled in the country of their origin. Each year men and women all over British Columbia come to Vancouver for that show; thousands of people attend. Mrs. McKay has trained the women, shown them how to bring their work to public notice, and helped many who otherwise would not have been able to show their work and sell it professionally to the general public.
This may be a small thing in relation to the thousands who are out of employment, but every little helps. The constant dropping wears away the stone. If more of us did what we could in that way, and if more women and the men themselves were encouraged by the government to help, irrespective of politics, we might in time solve part of our great problem of unemployment.
Yesterday afternoon I heard one hon. member say that every child born had just as much right to a living as the birds of the air. For the last month or six weeks I believe the birds of the air have been pretty busy on the grounds in front of this building, and it has been my experience with the birds of the air that they hope to scratch gravel or pull worms; nobody is going to do that work for them. I have stood and watched the robins brace themselves and pull until they get out a nice fat worm. I have watched the robins hopping around from bush to bush and tree to tree gathering the material to make nests.

The birds of the air have a right to a living, but like human beings they have to work for that living.
To the minister may I say, will he do the best he can to give our young people a chance for a living, a chance to work? The young man or young woman who is brought up without the discipline of work is no good to the community, no good to himself or herself. I look around on the hon. members of this house, young and old; the successful ones, the large majority of them, came from stock which forced the children out of the nest in early life; they are the ones we look up to. There have not been many men in this house during the time I have been watching since 1921 who had everything laid before them. So I say, if we can only give our young people that chance! Road building is good; we need good roads. Last spring, after the house adjourned, my husband and I motored to California. As we travelled through the states of Washington, Oregon and California I frequently made the remark: Your worst road that I have travelled over is better than the best we have in Canada. That may have been a little harsh to Canada. When I came east again this spring, I found the roads down there marvellous. Our best crop is the tourist crop. We want to harvest that crop every year. To do so we have to have good roads, and we must have good and sanitary accommodation for the tourists who come. The tourist from the south demands more than we in the north; I know full well, because I have lived practically half my life in bdth countries, or a little more than half my life here. I would say to the hon. member that I chose this country; I was not born here, but I chose it, and I have never regretted my choice. It has been a good country to live in; it has been good to me and my children, but I want to make it better for those who are to come after us. I feel sure that when he speaks of roads, housing and so on the minister wants to do all he can, but on the west coast-and I know Vancouver and that coast very well, since I have been going there for forty years-there are many people with monthly incomes of $150, $200 and up to $400, though they are not alwayg sure how long they are going to last. I ask hon. members here how those young people can raise their families of two to four and sometimes six children, and pay the taxes they would have to pay on the homes they would like to build. From my own experience I know that in the long run on that west coast it is much cheaper to rent than to build. That is too bad,

Relief and Agricultural Distress
because personally I would much prefer to live in a one, two or three roomed house that was my very own than be able to pay rent for a ten, twelve or fourteen roomed house. But the taxes are almost prohibitive; they prevent people from owning their own homes. That is another thing that must be looked after. We want our homes; we want our gardens; we want -every chance we can possibly have.
Then I should like to make just one suggestion to the minister. I do not intend to offer advice; God knows I am not fit to give anybody advice on this matter. When we think of the unemployment question and the matter of relief it seems to me that we are a good deal like the dog chasing its own tail. Just as we get hold of it the end slips away and we do not really know what to do. I have yet to meet a man or woman whom I could -pin down, who could conscientiously say to me, "Mrs. Black, I know what should be done," and then go on and tell me. They cannot do it. They can offer plenty of theories, but we do not want theories. The minister has a fearful task before him. A family may have lived in Quebec for twenty or twenty-five years. There may be illness or some other reason for a change. That family may come to Ontario, having run up against evil days. Are they going to receive relief here? No. They are Canadians, but Ontario is not going to help them. A family may have lived in the far north for forty years, grubbing away, working and living a dog's life. They come down to British Columbia, Alberta or Saskatchewan. Will they be helped? No, they can starve, unless they are helped through the generosity and kindliness of their neighbours. That is not right. We who vote these allowances do not belong to Quebec, Nova Scotia, the Yukon or British Columbia; we belong to all Canada. I firmly believe that the time must come when Canadians, as Canadians, will be helped if help is necessary, or will be given work-which is better than any relief that can be given- whether they come from the east or the west, the north or the south, so long as they are Canadians.
I wish to thank the minister especially, Mr. Chairman, for having listened so patiently to what I have had to say.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the hon. member for Yukon both for what she has said and for the very genuine and kindly manner in which she has said it. I am very sure her speech is one that ought to be recorded and preserved in the debates of this house. She has referred particularly
to the importance of the work done by individuals in making easier the lot of those who have suffered during recent years. I am very glad that she did so. Obviously one who holds the position of Minister of Labour cannot refer to individuals engaged in this work without making invidious comparisons; but certainly anyone who is aware of what has been going on during recent years will testify to the fact that without this voluntary work done by individuals, much of it by women, the policies of governments certainly would not have their full effect. I should like to thank the hon. member also for her other suggestions, and to assure her that I shall keep them in mind.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before we leave section 3 I should like to make a few observations which I hope the minister will receive in the kindly spirit that has been exhibited already this afternoon, and which I hope I may make in the spirit with which the previous speaker initiated the debate this afternoon.
I recognize the tremendous task with which the minister is confronted in connection with a problem of this nature. I know it is a complex problem, not easy of solution; and I for one would not wish to complicate the problem any further. But I should like to offer a few observations and suggestions in the hope that by some means the multitude of contributions made in this -house during this debate might eventually prove of some assistance in at least partially solving the problem. We recognize the magnitude of this question. When I consider the matter of unemployment in this country I often pause and compare it with our effort during war time periods. I consider that when we are faced with the problem of unemployment we are faced with a war within -our own borders, and I feel that the question of unemployment should be approached in the same way and with the same spirit that we would approach the problem of a real war. I know that if we were brought face to face with the question of going to war we would immediately plunge into that difficult task and see that it was successfully accomplished in the shortest possible time. There would be enough money properly and effectively to prosecute that war; we would not appoint a commission or committee, nor would we hesitate a moment in trying to bring to a successful conclusion the fight then on our hands.
I feel that the problem of unemployment might be approached in a somewhat similar fashion. We might throw ourselves into this



Relief and Agricultural Distress
fight within our borders with a great deal more vigour, and try to bring about a condition that, if it would not eliminate unemployment, at least would make it less severe than it is at the present time. We are now engaged in a war upon a social condition which has been very much aggravated by the recent depression. Talking about it will not eliminate it. Action must be undertaken, and I feel that we have been rather slow in undertaking that action.
I have already spoken on this question when the minister introduced the resolution on which this bill was based. On that occasion I brought to the attention of the government certain conditions with which I was not satisfied. To-day I want to approach this same subject from another angle, and I am asking the indulgence of the minister and of the committee if I seem somewhat tiring in the presentation of the facts and figures I want to place on Hansard. I wish particularly to place them before the minister and the government.
It is my view that the government should work in very much closer cooperation with the provinces, and I might add, although this might not meet with favour, with the muni-.ipalities. I know it is almost a recognized principle of government for the federal government not to deal too closely with the municipalities. But in a matter of this kind we are confronted with such serious possibilities that we must recognize the fact that municipal governments have a much more direct contact with the problem and with the people most concerned than either the provincial or the federal government. For that reason I do not believe the minister or the government in Ottawa should be adverse to receiving suggestions or delegations from municipalities, and particularly from those municipalities which have been most effective during the depression through which we have recently come in dealing with the unemployment which arose somewhat as a consequence of that depression.
I feel, too, that the government should not bear in mind the complexion of any provincial government with which it might be dealing. I am afraid there is sometimes the tendency in government to consider suggestions from the provinces in the light of the provinces from which the suggestions may come. I am afraid that provinces having governments which politically do not bear the same relation to this government as those in other provinces may not receive the same reception. In fact, that might be the reason for the attitude indicated in section 3 of the bill

now under consideration, which is somewhat different from the measures introduced last session and the session before.
Last year we discussed in the house the subjects of housing and slum clearance, problems which might adequately be faced at this time. Housing is a difficult problem, but one which offers a solution to unemployment, and a field to which we might go with some degree of hope for the eventual alleviation of distress through unemployment. I have in my hand a pamphlet read before an organization in Montreal by Professor Percy E. Nobbs of McGill university. Professor Nobbs, as most hon. members know, is recognized as an authority on town planning, slum clearance, housing and problems of that kind. At the beginning of his address he quoted from the observations of Henry Vivian, also a world recognized authority in the same field. Mr. Vivian's concluding observations were that in most Canadian towns-
-less science and forethought are given to the care of human beings than the modern farmer gives to the raising of his pigs.
That is a strong statement, but I believe it is a good introduction to a discussion of housing and slum clearance. I should like to quote further from the observations of Professor Nobbs. What he states has direct reference to Montreal, but would apply equally to any large city in Canada. He said:
As I have been pointing out for years, Montreal is notably deficient in low rental dwellings when the numbers of low wage earners in the community are taken account of. There has never been any concerted attempt to house our workers. Now we find that while rental values for superior accommodation are still going down, or are still as low as they ever have been since the war, the rental values of the poorest accommodation in the city are rising. During the first years of the depression, the Montreal proprietors housed the unemployed rent free. With the institution of unemployment relief, the unemployed were accommodated in $25 a month dwellings at $12 rents. Those dwellings are now better rented and the Unemployment Relief Commission has entered the market for lower rental property. I shall not say whether the next fact to be disclosed is a matter of cause or effect, but there is a notable tendency to the consolidation of this class of property, rented to the Unemployment Commission, in fewer hands month by month. So if ever there -was a case for large-scale, low rent housing operations, that case exists in Montreal to-day. for there is a shortage of dwellings of all classes, from $50 a month rentals, downwards, and the shortage of dwellings renting from $14 to $9 is most acute.
That is what Professor Nobbs said after a very careful study of conditions existing in Montreal. With what he has to say I am in hearty agreement; in fact, I am in complete accord. It was my privilege to spend

Relief and Agricultural Distress
some time in the office of the metropolitan commission in Montreal where, with one of the directors, Mr. George Mooney, a gentleman well known to my friends immediately to my left, we studied the problem of slum clearance and housing. He pointed out definite spots on the map of Montreal where projects could be commenced immediately to the advantage of the city, the workers and those at present unemployed. He deplored the fact that nothing of a concrete nature was being pushed forward at the present time in the larger cities.
While I speak with direct reference to Montreal I have in mind that there are other large cities and towns in Canada. I have no doubt that what has been said respecting Montreal could be said with equal force about Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver, or any of the other larger centres. It is my hope therefore that under section 3, where the minister contemplates certain works of a public nature, slum clearance and housing with rental values from $10 to $15 per month may be undertaken, so that people who are forced to live in accommodation of that kind may obtain it and may live as decent human beings desire to live.
Reference has been made to unemployment insurance. My recollection is that one of the first speeches I made in the house was concerning that subject. I am just as strongly in favour of unemployment insurance to-day as I was at that time, although I do recognize certain weaknesses. I make that statement despite the tirade against unemployment insurance lodged by one of the social credit members last night. He did not convince me in any way that the workers of Canada were making any mistake in urging the institution of unemployment insurance. I know the difficulties with which the minister has been confronted in connection with this question. I know, too, it has been decided by the courts that unemployment insurance is within the provincial field of jurisdiction. But I know he recognizes, I recognize and every hon. member recognizes that it is a question with which it is quite impossible for provincial governments to deal. It is a question of national importance; it is a question that will have to be faced eventually and solved by a national government sitting at Ottawa.
I have in my hand a report that was issued in the United States of America in connection with the social security act recently passed in Washington. I notice that this report refers to a possible solution of the unemployment insurance problem. It states that the social security act can be divided into two 51952-1581
distinct parts, the first being the old age retirement benefits, which are contributions collected from both the employers and the employees, and the second being the unemployment insurance benefits, which are provided for employees out of contributions paid in those states which have unemployment insurance laws. The social security act is designed to induce the states to adopt such laws. I know the minister is as fully conversant with this document and with that act as I am. After reading certain sections of the social security act as passed in the United States and as adopted by many of the states of the union I feel that there is a possibility of solving our problem along that line without the necessity of altering the British North America Act in any way.
I know that certain provinces are not opposed to unemployment insurance as such, but they are opposed to anything that might be interpreted as an easy way to amend the British North America Act. They like to feel that that act is almost impossible of amendment. For this reason we should try to find another means of approach so that unemployment insurance can be brought into being and put into effect without causing any offence to any provincial government, whether it be a Social Credit government in Alberta, a Union Nationale government in Quebec, or a Liberal government in New Brunswick. I feel sure the minister is giving serious thought to the possibilities of action along this line.
I have also in my hand an extract from an article written by a great friend of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who is personally well known to the Minister of Labour. I refer to Mr. Bernard Rose, K.C., a prominent lawyer in the city of Montreal. Writing in Le Monde Ouvrier under date of April 23, 1938, he states:
Mr. King positively pledged his party to adopt a national contributory system of unemployment insurance if he was elected. Having the utmost confidence in the word and pledge of the Prime Minister, hundreds of thousands of voters throughout the dominion cast their ballots in favour of his party's candidates.
He continues with his article and towards the close he states:
I would hazard the opinion that the government, in view of the situation and promoting public welfare, is constitutionally justified in enacting the measure under the "peace, order and good government" clause of the British North America Act.
Remember, this article is written by a lawyer in Montreal who has always been a supporter of the Liberal party. It sounds rather strange to hear the words "peace, order and good

Relief and Agricultural Distress
government" mentioned as a foundation for an enactment by one who pretends to be of Liberal persuasion. Nevertheless he uses these words in good faith and I refer this article to the minister. It continues:
If any one or more provinces were dissatisfied the onus of constitutional attack would be upon them.
. That is written by a gentleman who presumes to be and who is I believe an authority on the matter. He is known to the Minister of Labour and has done special work for the Department of Labour from time to time. He has been actively engaged in labour movements from the time he was able to take part in any movement. He gives it as his opinion that unemployment insurance can be brought into effect by this government should they desire to take action under that oft-repeated clause of peace, order and good government. He believes that should this action be challenged in the courts, the decision would be that the point was not well taken and that the government was within its rights in passing legislation under that particular clause. I read with a great deal of interest in today's Hansard the remarks of the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) and also those of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and for the most part I am in accord with their particular reference to unemployment and their suggestions along that line. They are rather vigorous in their criticism of the policies of the present government and the lack of anything definite or concrete actually before us. In discussing this bill, I for one cannot see why the Minister of Labour cannot stand before parliament and, instead of telling us to wait for the supplementary estimates or to wait for something before disclosing the whole program, give us in concise terms exactly what his department proposes to do in order to carry out the provisions of the bill that we are now studying. I do not think it is asking him to do too much to take the members of the house into his confidence, because they are deeply interested in what the government are going to do in the immediate future. I know he proposes to make that statement before the house rises, probably when the other estimates are before the house; but here is an important bill, and many members have expressed a desire to know exactly what the government intends to do. The minister should be in a position now to express an opinion and to give the house very definite information as to what he has in mind at the present time in regard to employment relief in Canada. I hope that before the debate concludes he will have a detailed statement ready to present to us.
It was rather gratifying to listen to the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood) last evening. He brings with him into debate a wholesome atmosphere, and in my opinion, if there were more solid, staid Canadian citizens like him this country would be better off and we would have less unemployment. I rather like his complimentary remarks to the Minister of Labour and his sympathy with him as he listens from day to day to the debates in this house, particularly on this measure, and I hope that the minister will take cognizance of what the hon. gentleman had to say, especially the commonsense point of view he gave to the house in reference to many of the suggestions that are indirectly referred to in this bill. I have already referred to the fact that the building trade was the one most seriously injured. The member for Brant last evening made reference to higher wages being paid in the city, and he did not think that was a cure

for unemployment. I want to assure him that the country is always more prosperous when higher wages are paid in the cities. Thereby more purchasing power is put into the cities to relieve the agricultural population of their produce at a higher price than they would otherwise obtain.

I prefer to talk in terms
which the workingman can understand. I am referring to the money that is put into the pay envelopes of men who are empiloyed for seven, eight and nine hours a day. When those wages are high you put greater purchasing power into the hands of the workers and they are able to use it to advantage, and as they use it agriculture and other industries develop and thrive. On the other hand, if you put low purchasing power in the worker's hands it depreciates the products of other people who are engaged in either primary or secondary industry. That is a well-recognized fact.

look at it from the broad point of view of the workers.

speechtext:
You have to take the wage of any particular class and compare it with what is paid for the services of other people in similar walks of life. It is no use arguing

Relief and Agricultural Distress
the point; it is obvious to anyone who will give it proper attention. The question must be looked at not from any narrow point of view, not only from the point of view of the workers, but from the point of view of every Canadian citizen who is interested in the maximum distribution of money, wages paid in the country. If we can get that maximum distribution there will be little or no unemployment.
I have in my hand the "Report of the Investigation Committee re Unemployment", in the city of Montreal, and I notice certain very broad features in connection with the building trade. I see that from 1925 down to 1936 there was at first an increase up to the year 1929 from 825,000,000 to $46,000,000, in the total amount of building being done in the city. Then it gradually decreased until in 1936 it had gone down to $6,905,323. I read these figures in order to emphasize the tremendous decrease in building operations in the city of Montreal alone, and that accounts for a large part of the unemployment, and hence the number on direct relief. That is why I urge slum clearance and a cheaper housing program for the larger centres in order to stimulate industry in the building trades. If we make a comparison between January 1 and May 31, we find that there was an increase from $1,698,067 in 1936 to $2,992,235 in 1937. On the same page, under the heading Loan Facilities, the statement is made:
Statistics of the last three years show that while savings are gradually increasing by 900 millions per year, loans to business and money in circulation are constantly decreasing. Means shuld be taken to prevent this decrease.
Again looking at the "Report of the Investigation Committee re Unemployment", city of Montreal, page 29, we find that in 1936 deposits in bank savings amounted to 818,218,588,511; loans to business in the same year amounted to 88,384,277,880; money in circulation in the same year amounted to $1,434,067,677. If we compare that with 1935 and 1934 we find a decrease in loans, showing that we are gradually receding as far as loan facilities are concerned. And that is not in any way helping to make matters better as far as Montreal is concerned. These observations are not made in the spirit of political criticism; I did indulge in that when the minister first introduced his motion covering this bill, and I felt I was justified in doing so on that occasion. But to-day I wanted to put before the minister these facts with particular reference to the city of Montreal, not only because I am particularly interested in that city but also on account of it being a centre from
which I could get direct and authentic information, and knowing that conclusions drawn from that authentic information could be applied to other large centres in Canada. I urge upon the minister the necessity of giving serious consideration to a slum clearance program in the larger cities, and the building of low rental houses.
Have we had tabled in the house any report of the employment commission in connection with low rental houses, or slum clearance, or both? If not, will such a report be tabled? For I understand that the employment commission made a very complete study of general conditions not only in Canada and the United States but also in Great Britain and some European countries. I know there is reference to it, but I wonder if a complete and detailed report, making certain suggestions and recommendations, has been before the government but has not yet been placed before this house, something on which we could base an argument for immediate action which would bring alleviation to the building trades of this country.

That does contain to my knowledge the entire plan submitted by the national employment commission with respect to low rental housing.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The debate on this bill has extended over a considerable length of time, and been characterized by repeated demands and continued pressure upon the minister for more information and for details of the program he has in mind. We have had before this house seven or perhaps eight bills for the relief of unemployment. Reviewing them all and looking now at Bill No. 105 at present before this committee, I fail to find in any of these bills very many differences in the general scheme and outline and plan proposed for the relief of unemployment. I recall that in years gone by when bills such as this were
Relief and Agricultural Distress

first introduced there was strong pressure, carried to extreme limits, for details, estimates, statements of policy. I submit that after this lapse of time, and after the setting up of an employment commission whose investigation covered at least a year and cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, hon. -members are not unreasonable in pressing the minister for a more detailed and more expanded program than has been presented in the past. I submit in all seriousness that at this stage we have a right to ask the minister for much more information, much more detail, much fuller explanation of the plans of the government for the coming year-if they have any

than hitherto we have had.
One criticism in particular of the bills brought in from 1931 to 1935 was, as the minister well knows, that they were in the nature of a blank cheque; that they gave to the governor in council authority and discretion to do practically anything and everything. I ask the -minister to compare this bill with the others and to point out, if he can, how it materially differs in that respect from any of its predecessors.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The matter of parliamentary appropriations, of course, is a material difference.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I do not think that makes a bit of difference.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: It bears directly on the blank cheque question.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I -think not. I expected the minister to make that point. We have parliamentary appropriations with respect to certain items, not all. But where do -parliamentary appropriations come from? They come fro-m the governor in council; it is the governor in council who places before this house estimates of what is to be expended.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: But there is a limitation upon them.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: This bill says that the governor in council shall determine what expenditures shall be made out of moneys which are provided by the governor in council. What authority has any hon. member of this house to increase or modify by one dollar the appropriations made by the governor in council?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The appropriation is a limitation. With a blank cheque there is no limitation. Surely that is a material difference. Under the blank cheque legislation

there was no limitation of any kind, with respect either to the amount or to the direction of expenditure.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
It is a distinction without a difference; for there is no limitation now upon w-hat the governor in council may place in those estimates. The estimates for this purpose may be $20,000,000, $50,000,000 or $100,000,000; there is no limitation. So in the end it is fixed by the governor in council, and it is the governor in council that has control of it. In section 3 I find these words:
The governor in council may out of moneys appropriated by parliament authorize the execution of such undertakings as the governor in council may determine-
Then in subsection 2 of the sa-me section:
In the execution of any such undertaking provision shall be made, so far as it may be in the opinion of the governor in council practical and consistent with reasonable efficiency-
And -so on. Then in section 4:
The governor in council may enter into agreements-[DOT]
Then follow two or three subdivisions. Then section 5:
The governor in council, where necessary, may out of any unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund grant financial assistance to any province-
And so on. Then in subsection 2 of section 5:
The governor in council may renew or consolidate for such periods and upon such terms as the governor in council may determine, loans, advances

And so on. Then further on in the same section:
-may accept such treasury bills, bonds, debentures or other securities as may be approved by the governor in council-
Then in section 7:
The governor in council may make all such orders and regulations as may be deemed necessary or desirable to carry out the purposes and intentions of this act.
Section 8 provides:
All orders and regulations of the governor in council . . . shall have the force of law and may be varied, extended or revoked-
Then section 10:
Subject to the approval of the governor in council the minister may appoint such officers, clerks and employees

So it is my contention that in all essential respects and for all practical purposes, considering that the estimates in the first instance are determined and settled by the governor in council, the administration of the act and the amount to be expended under it are

Relief and Agricultural Distress
within the control of the governor in council. In that respect it does not differ from previous bills, and I do not see how it could well differ. It is difficult to ascertain or anticipate what may be the requirements, and under the circumstances the governor in council must have a wide discretion. I am simply mentioning this in answer to the criticism of years gone by in regard to the policy that was adopted.
As I have said, the minister has been pressed for information. It seems to me that if he had adopted the course that was followed last year his position would have been much better to-day. Last year the special supplementary estimates which accompanied a similar bill were tabled in the house at a comparatively early date. According to the journals of the house they were brought down on March 3, and from that time on the members of the house had before them details of the expenditures proposed by the government for these purposes. A summary of those estimates shows that $19,000,000 odd was included for grants in aid. In going through these estimates one finds large items, such as must be expended under the terms of this bill. For instance, there was item 302, under the Department of Labour: To provide for federal contribution to provincial and municipal relief projects, $7,000,000 odd. Item 304: To provide for federal contribution to farm employment and supplementary plans, $3,000,000 odd.. Item 308: To provide for development and training projects for unemployed young people, $1,000,000. Item 309: To provide for direct relief in the dried out areas, $2,000,000. Then: Grants in aid: amount required to provide for monthly grants in aid to the provinces, $19,500,000. So, as I have mentioned, every member of this house had information as to the amount which would be available for expenditure during the coming year under the provisions of the bill.
The second reading of the bill similar to the one we are now considering did not take place until March 31, 1937. Now, for some reason which the minister may be able or may desire to explain, a different course has been followed. This house is asked to consider and pass this bill in this blanket form, without information similar to that which was furnished last year; without any estimates before it and with the knowledge that when the estimates do come down they cannot be increased by one dollar. Under these circumstances I ask the minister if he thinks the members of this committee are acting
unreasonably in pressing for this information. Here we are in the month of May. We ought to be beginning work for the relief of unemployment, but we have not the estimates before us. Last year we had them on March 3, and it was possible to consider the bill in the light of those estimates. Why was not a similar course adopted this year? Cannot the government make up their minds, with the report of the employment commission before them? Why are they withholding from this house their plans, their program, their intentions, and a statement of the amount of money that they expect to expend for the relief of unemployment during 1938? That is what the members of this committee wish to know. That is what they are pressing for, and I do submit to the minister that the position they are taking is fair and reasonable, and the only one that will enable the committee to come to a conclusion as to whether the plans proposed are adequate or inadequate; whether they are sufficiently broad and comprehensive.
I had hoped that in view of the statements of the minister on previous occasions we would have had presented a plan covering more than one year. The minister has spoken of a long range program, but here we have the same old proposition. This act expires March 31, 1939. There is no provision, no plan, no scheme, no program except a temporary makeshift one for the year 1938. There is no housing plan, so far as we know. I do suggest to the minister that we might embark upon a program to cover more than one year, for the construction of highways, particularly in connection with secondary roads rather than main highways, of which we have perhaps enough for the time being.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Would not my hon. friend
think that secondary roads, even more than main highways, -were principally a provincial responsibility?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
That may be so, but each year it is growing more difficult to draw the line between federal, provincial and municipal responsibility, and to divide the work and the cost of unemployment relief. I do suggest that at this time there is less cooperation among the municipalities, the provinces and the dominion than there ever was, so far as unemployment relief is concerned. All one has to do is to take note of what he reads in the press. There we find evidence that some of the provincial authorities criticize the dominion government for evading responsibilities, and the municipalities criticize provincial and federal governments for the same
Relief and Agricultural Distress

reason. To my mind it has become at least to a certain extent-and I do not use the term offensively-a process of chiselling, where each one sees how much it can get from the other.
I believe we are driven to find any field of employment in which men can usefully be set to work. We cannot draw the line too finely as to whether it is municipal, provincial or federal. Reforestation and works of that kind might be undertaken as a program not for one year-that is the point I am impressing upon the minister-but extending over several years. In view of the statements made by the minister respecting plans, and in view of the visions he had outlined of a program covering a long-range attack, I had expected something greater than a program for only one year. I would suggest that it be laid out for a number of years, and that enough money be appropriated to make available a certain amount over a period of five years to overtake the work. There is enough useful work to be done in Canada to extend over that length of time, and I would urge the minister to consider something of the kind.
Almost every criticism has been advanced, and it is not my desire to take up further time. I do not wish to embarrass the minister in connection with the problem before him for solution, but I do say that if he had adopted the course followed last year and had brought - down estimates much time would have been saved, much information would have been available and we would have had some understanding of the plan the government intends to follow, a plan which at present is obscure and about which we know practically nothing. If one were to carry out the program suggested by the hon. member who has just spoken, there would not result in any substantial measure any real relief. I suggest to the minister that when he comes to consider what shall be done by way of works for those areas which find themselves in the greatest distress he should bear in mind, as undoubtedly he will, the need of providing work in those centres where work in temporary form is required most. A great road scheme, meritorious as it may be, would not be of very much assistance to the city from which I come. I cannot speak for Toronto, Hamilton and other industrial cities; but my impression is that a large road building scheme, while it may give work to many who probably need it, will not provide the same opportunities for others who undoubtedly need it most, I do not think one can stress this point too much.
I have sat through this entire debate; I do not believe I have left the house for ten minutes; and my earlier intention was to say something which now has already been said by many hon. members. I therefore wish merely to make this suggestion. The problem is particularly acute at this time, although not so acute as some have made it out to be. This condition exists, not so much because of what this government has failed to do, not so much because of what the previous government failed to do, but because when this country enjoyed prosperity we failed to take precautions to deal with a
state of unemployment which has been traditional with us almost throughout our history. The right hon. leader of the opposition yesterday interjected a remark that in this respect unemployment was essentially a seasonal matter. That I think is true. I mention this, not with the purpose of suggesting extenuating circumstances for the minister or for the government, but as a fact which must be borne in mind in trying to meet this problem.
I suggest to the minister that either we are going to do something about this problem of unemployment or we are not; either we are going to spend the people's money in an effort to temporize with this problem or we are not. If we are going to take out of the public exchequer funds with which to provide in an artificial way employment for those who do not have it, we should do so in an effective manner; otherwise the economic waste, let alone the disastrous results which must follow from an attempt to impress upon sections of the unemployed that the government intends to take care of them when in the final resort the government for some reason or none finds that it cannot, will have more serious consequences than the attempt which has already been indicated.
I have tried, as I sat in this house during the last few days, to think of something to suggest to the minister that he does not already know, but I am afraid there is nothing I can say that he does not already know. The speeches that have already been given probably cover the entire ground. But I do suggest, in view of the brief presented yesterday by the Ontario government, that the record of practically every country in the western world in respect of unemployment insurance should convince this country of the need for it. The question arises whether we are to have unemployment insurance at the initiative of the provinces or of the federal government. My view is that unemployment is a national problem and that it is for this parliament to deal with it. I quite appreciate the attitude which will undoubtedly be taken by areas wherein the population is essentially rural and not urban. But I suggest that the economy of Canada is such that we cannot make distinct differentials in respect of geographical divisions. It is true one can speak of the western provinces, but in doing so one must not forget that that region contains cities. In British Columbia, of course, is the great city of Vancouver; in the maritime provinces there is Halifax as well as other large centres. To talk of unemployment insurance in terms

of only two provinces will not, in my judgment, adequately meet this problem of unemployment. I am particularly interested in unemployment insurance, for this reason. The workers in many of the factories of Windsor, for instance, are not employed for the full year. They will work for five, six, seven or eight months and then they are thrown out of work. In many oases they have to be maintained by the state, through the agency of the municipality or otherwise. That condition cannot go on forever. The longer we postpone action the more difficult it is going to be. Fully appreciative as I am of the great labour and sincerity the minister has put into his job, I suggest to him that it will be a matter of deep satisfaction to the people of Canada, and certainly to the area from which I come, if before this parliament rises we shall have at least taken steps to initiate a scheme of national unemployment insurance.

Just a few remarks in reference to some statements made by the last speaker. In regard to unemployment insurance he said he favoured the idea of the government enacting legislation and taking a chance to see whether it was constitutional or otherwise. The hon. member, who is a lawyer and a student of constitutional problems, knows that is exactly what was done in 1935; upon the change of government the party now in power tested the validity of that legislation, and it was declared by the highest court in the empire to be unconstitutional. So if the present government followed that suggestion, we should be in the same position as we were at the beginning of 1936.
The hon. member, however, suggested other alternatives. He proposed that this government enact legislation along the lines of the Old Age Pensions Act, making it pennissive for the various provinces to come in. If the government would make an act of that kind sufficiently attractive, I think many provinces, if not all, would elect to come under the operation of such an act. Whether or not it is advisable to do so, I cannot say. Another alternative is along the lines of legislation enacted in the United States, where they are confronted with the same constitutional difficulty. That country has also adopted permissive legislation, and I observe that at the present time nearly all the states have come within the provisions of the social security act enacted there. Then there is another alternative which I suggest, although I have not given it very serious consideration. In view of what was said by the premier of Ontario before the Rowell commission, there seems to be a good deal of conflict as to jurisdiction, as to which authority should undertake certain legislation. In certain provinces the idea seems to be that more power should be given to the provinces. But in regard to such questions as old age pensions and unemployment insurance I think it would be admitted on all sides that they are federal matters. Perhaps
kMr. Martin.]
it would be well for us in this parliament to consider whether there should not be a national referendum on the question whether such problems as this should not be entirely under federal jurisdiction, and this federal parliament have the right- to amend the constitution, giving to the federal authorities the right to legislate on such matters as unemployment insurance. I think if such a referendum were held it would show that the overwhelming sentiment of the electors of Canada is in favour of giving to the federal authorities the right to legislate on such matters. If that were done, we might once and for all do away with the conflict as to jurisdiction in matters of this kind.
Personally I am anxious to see the government enact legislation in regard to unemployment insurance. But even that is not in itself a sufficient remedy for the difficulties facing us at the present time. As pointed out so ably by the speaker who preceded me, in the city of Windsor many men work for only eight months in the year. It would be almost impossible to keep a scheme of unemployment insurance actuarially sound under such conditions, maintaining those people for the other four months of the year. Consequently, we have to go far beyond the. mere question of insurance, and provide public relief works or private sustenance, as at present. However, I just rose to say that I am extremely anxious to see if the government cannot now find ways and means of doing something towards bringing into being a scheme of unemployment insurance. I fully realize the constitutional difficulties in the way, but if the government, even at this late date, with all the knowledge they have at their command and their skilled experts, brought in a comprehensive scheme, I am sure that ultimately the people of this country would commend the government for such action.

I should like to pay the same tribute to the right hon. leader of the opposition and the late government. There is no one in Canada who does not realize the extraordinary ability and industry which the former Prime Minister brought to the conduct of the affairs of the nation. I say that simply because we in this comer believe that the trouble is not with governments; it is with the system which governments administer, just as Mr. Hawtrey says. That system breaks government after government; more than that, it is breaking the institution of parliamentary government itself. People are losing faith in the power or ability of parliament to achieve anything. There is no doubt of that, and the question is whether we are going to put the needs of the people first or whether we are going to put the needs of the financial system first. No man can serve two masters; neither can a government. They cannot serve the people and at the same time serve the financial interests.
When we come to unemployment we know, because we have recent history to back us up, that if we wanted to we could abolish unemployment to-morrow. We did it once, and no member of this house can deny it. During the war there was no unemployment, and if

Relief and Agricultural Distress
war came again there would be no unemployment at that time Why? There is only one answer; it is that in the danger with which the country is confronted in the face of the enemy, all other considerations are put to one side; they must give way to the supreme duty of preserving the safety of the nation. In such times money is put to its proper use, and the financier is put in his proper place. Parliament asserts its real authority, and the money is found. It does not matter where or how it is found; it is found, and we could do the same in regard to unemployment if we wanted to. But we cannot do it and still preserve what is known as sound money, or, in other words, scarce money. That, as I see it, is the issue before the country. We can either preserve what we call sound money and sound economics, or we can adapt our economic system to a different age so that the people of Canada may be able to consume all they care to produce. When we do that we shall solve unemployment, and not before.
As for unemployment insurance, I am not going to say much against it. If the people want it, let them have it; but to my mind you might just, as well take a case of smallpox and send it to a beauty parlour. Unemployment is not the disease; it is the symptom of a disease, and until we attack the disease, itself I do not think we can get very far with the symptom.
Those are all the observations I wish to make at this time. I know hon. members in this section of the house are laughed and jeered at, but I have heard nothing in or out of the house to check my belief in what we in this corner of the house say. If there are other remedies I should like to hear them, but so far I have not heard anything which offers a real remedy to the problem with which this and other countries are confronted to-day.

When I hear hon. members opposite talk about the terrible strain and anxiety they have to carry, and when I hear the fulsome adulation with which followers refer to the government and to the ministers, I recall days when those same hon. gentlemen, sitting to the left of the Speaker, could not find time enough in which to express themselves, or language strong enough to ex-oress the condemnation of those who were endeavouring to do the very thing that the present government is now endeavouring to do. Let there be no mistake: Except with

respect to one insignificant expenditure there has been not the slighest change in everything that has been done by the department in connection with unemployment and relief. Every single thing that is being done to-day was being done by the late administration, except the work in connection with the so-called youth movement, about which we will speak when the proper time comes.
Yet the student of history, in reading Hansard from 1930 to 1935, will find that the men now occupying the treasury benches were then spending their hours, days and weeks in condemnation of the then government for doing what they now do. As I hear these observations, and the sympathy that is being extended; when I compare the buoyant revenues of to-day with the revenues of those days, and when I think of the changed world conditions as compared with the conditions of those days, I wonder where their milk of human sympathy and kindness was to be found. I bring that fact to the attention of the committee this afternoon. There is no reason why the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) should look sadder than anybody else, although I must admit he was one of the chief offenders.

We are told we must accept them as the great contribution of far-sighted statesmen in dealing with these problems.
If it ended there, it might not be quite so bad. But the historian of this country will also find that the present government when in opposition was going to take this whole problem out of the realm of politics, and that an independent commission was going to administer relief; an independent commission was going to correlate the activities of the provinces and the dominion; an independent commission was going to deal with the municipalities, and their difficulties with relation to the provincial and federal powers. The commission has gone out of business, and the same political administration which marked the administration of the days in which control was vested in the government still prevails.
The great evil that -we face to-day in the administration of unemployment relief is found in political patronage, about which, at the proper time, I propose to say much. There is not a day which does not bring me letters from men who are unable to find employment because they have not the proper sanction, the sanction of those who sit in authority either as defeated candidates, or otherwise, for the purpose of determining whether men shall or shall not have jobs. One park in this country is run by the Liberal party executive, and men are dismissed from their positions and other men put in their places for the purpose of enabling them to circumvent the law. That is what is going on. I spoke yesterday about Long Branch; I could name other places as well. I could mention place after place in which either the defeated candidate, the head of the Liberal association in the locality, or someone else, must be consulted before it is possible for a man to find employment, for which he is paid with my taxes and the taxes of other taxpayers in this country. That is the reason that this thing fails- and it is failing. Of course it is failing. The hon. member who judt took his seat referred to the fact that we are not dealing with the disease. In my place yonder between 1930 and 1935 I pointed out that these measures were palliatives, not cures. They do not cure the disease; they are but palliatives. Every thoughtful man knows that is so. Everyone knows perfectly well, sir, that with respect to the problem of unemployment we must realize it can never be dealt with in the manner which is being followed.
Who, listening to the political speech in connection with farm implements the other evening, but must realize that in this country we have a population over one-half of which is in urban areas. Remember that. No longer is half or more than half of the population in rural communities. This means that unless we supply that urban population with employment measures there will be constant unemployment. There is no thoughtful member of parliament who does not realize that the essential obligation resting upon the house at this time is to provide employment for our people by submitting policies which will ensure that there is work to do.

In other words, a substantial part of the population believes it is better to have immediate benefit in contemplation-not reality-than to have some measure of cure effected with respect to the disease from which we are suffering.
You cannot have your goods manufactured for you in another country, give employment to people in that country and at the same time not put out of employment those who are doing the work here. Let there be no misunderstanding about that fundamental. You may differ from me on the particular problems connected with the fiscal policy of a country. We may differ; but we cannot differ about this, that if the consuming population of Canada requires for its use and sustenance a million dollars worth of goods, and those goods can be made in this country, then unless we afford the opportunity for the people who have now flocked to the cities tc engage in industrial life they will be unemployed, while people somewhere else will be employed. They will make the very goods that we consume. There can be no misunderstanding about that. It was all right when you had the great majority of your people on the land; it was all right when the major part of your population was rural, but our population has shifted. The other evening the hon. member for Jacques-Cartier (Mr. Mallette) referred to the population that had shifted from the soil to the city. This has brought about a condition which we must face. That condition involves action being taken of a kind that apparently some of our friends dislike.
This government is in a position to make its choice. It has behind it a majority that enables it to make any choice it pleases and to give effect to that choice. It has made its choice. It has balanced the probabilities. It has selected one particular way of dealing with the matter. What has been the result? This is not the time, or the place perhaps, to deal with it in detail. A vested right may be lost by expropriation, for instance. That is one way in which it may be lost. Then, it might be lost by agreement between the parties; that is the usual method by which it is disposed of. I am pointing out that in this case a vested right in the United States is a right which, by action of this parliament, extends beyond the boundary of the United States. That is, our parliament has become a party to the union of rights that enabled the bridge to be built on the Canadian side, with the power exercised in the state of New York that had to do with its commencement in that state. Under the law of the state of New York they cannot, if they will, according to counsel's opinion-and in my judgment that is the law, but that does not add to the weight of it- interfere with the constitutional rights of those who possess vested rights. The state may take it. That right is called the power of eminent domain in some countries, the power of expropriation in others. The arrangement and agreement for compensation would dispose of vested rights satisfactorily. The power of expropriation is a power which I believe has been exercised by Ontario on more than one occasion.

We have this wonderful spectacle of Conservative members from Ontario doing their 'best to see that their own province cannot build a bridge which it desires to build. I should hate to be in their shoes when they go back to Ontario to ask the people for support in the next election. I think I know what the people will say should they find that those hon. members have been successful in blocking this bill.
I ask the committee to look at the other side of the matter. Of all the persons who might come here to ask for the right to build a bridge, who would be the most logical? The province of Ontario. Why does not, the province of Ontario ask directly for this
Niagara Falls Bridge

right? Apparently it cannot. Certain individuals are named in the bill, and these individuals have shown their good faith and intentions by giving an assignment to the province of Ontario or the Niagara parks commission. If that is illegal, as has been inferred by the leader of the opposition, then it would have no effect. So far as this bill is concerned, there is no assignment in its provisions. According to the best legal advice at our disposal, this bill could not be drafted in any other form.
This committee has listened to objections to the province of Ontario constructing a bridge to connect its roadway system with the other side of the river. speechtext:
When the committee rose at six o'clock I was reading a portion of a resolution that had been adopted by the greater Vancouver youth council with respect to slum clearance in that city. I had concluded reading the second recital of the resolution. The third recital proceeds:
And whereas:-This conference, here assembled, representing a large cross-section of public opinion is unanimously agreed that there can be no solution to the problem without government intervention.
And whereas:-A large scale economically sound housing program under government restriction and supervision would be the means of stimulating the building construction trade and providing a substantial increase in employment.
Therefore be it resolved: that the federal parliament now assembled be urged to give this matter immediate consideration and to enact legislation necessary to provide adequate housing for people with low incomes.
And further be it resolved: that this resolution be forwarded to all B.C. representatives in the federal house and the responsible authorities at Ottawa.
I read that merely for the purpose of directing attention to the fact that throughout Canada there is a widespread impression that if we embarked on a large low priced housing scheme we would do something for the solution of the problem of unemployment. It is a resolution similar in terms to that which has been passed in most of the great cities of the country, in somewhat different terms, according to the city in which it was passed or the group which sponsored it.
But there is another view also to which attention might be directed; and as that view has not been presented to the committee, I thought it might be well for me to do so, as indicating that the dearth of houses in some of our cities is said to be because of the change of style with respect to our houses. The following letter received by me from British Columbia directs attention to this: lie wish to very strongly protest against further government competition in home building, especially low rental ideas.
It is not fair to penalize one class for the benefit of others.
Hundreds of people have worked very hard and saved their money, investing it in homes 51952-160
and rental property so that they and their families would not become public charges in ill health and old age.
It used to be work and save. Now it is do little and spend. This is gradually becoming a nation of mendicants. Poverty used to be a disgrace and people hid it*-now it seems to be something to brag about.
Certain interests-some selfishly, others thoughtlessly-are fostering ideas of a housing shortage without regard to the eventual outcome. Regardless of what they report there is no acute shortage. One has only to pick up the papers to see plenty of houses for sale and for rent all the way across the dominion. Rentals are greatly reduced, it is becoming increasingly harder to get renters and they are demanding more and more.
These people who have built up the country and are its very backbone built at high prices and have had to spend thousands of dollars in increasingly higher taxes and maintenance (labour and material) all through these trying times. Now they are to be sacrificed in order that the great lending companies can get a safe outlet for their hoarded millions, and with government backing; and that the lower class might be properly housed-a class as a whole who has contributed very little in actual dollars to the upkeep of the country.

. 1 be spirit of fear has entered private initiative, they are trying to unload and refuse to further invest. You surely must realize that private enterprise is what actually makes a healthy prosperous country.

Governments earn nothing. They can only rob Peter to pay Paul. And unless restraint is exercised, the day comes when the plundering process becomes no longer possible.''
Let me quote from a letter from a New Yorker who is very well informed and who has been in business there for years. I think that it very adequately gives the facts.
Really I am reading this part of the communication because of that quotation, and it is an amazing quotation: I have not before seen it:
"You mentioned housing shortage, but there just isn't any such thing. The truth of the matter is that style trends in houses are partly responsible for a peculiar situation. New York anyway is overstocked with old-fashioned houses and apartments. No one wants to buy an old-fashioned type of house, without the latest in tiled bathrooms, modernistic kitchen and oil or gas heating plant. The same is true with apartments. Large ones of five, six or seven rooms are a drug on the market, and all the older type are large. Consequently people keep vacating the houses, and in many cases being unable to sell them, board them up, and the older apartment houses that aren't salable are being boarded up. Why isn't there a wholesale pulling down of old houses and putting up what people want, you will say. Because those who own the old property want to get something out of it-they want to sell it for whatever cash they can get and apparently there is no disposition on the part of those who lend to do so until they unload their holdings. Families are living with their relatives in increasing numbers because jobs are so difficult to get that a young man can't think of getting married and going out and buying a house. It is true that if all the young people living with relatives were to go out and want to buy a house, there would be a housing shortage. But the trouble is they haven't got the money and in the second place they would be afraid to buy a house right now if they did have it. So in New York at least there is a great deal more property idle than I have ever seen, including business property. In downtown New York, whole buildings are vacant and the trend is toward the merger of two firms because neither is making money, with the consolidation of both in one office, leaving the other vacant. Uptown there is plenty of office space available too. It is a standing joke about the inability of the Empire State building to rent most of its space."
There are plenty of public works crying to be done-roads for tourist traffic and our own travelling public. Etc., etc. Give people jobs and food and clothing and housing will take care of themselves.	_ _
You are the opposition, of course, but politics must be forgotten when it comes to cancers starting to eat at the very vitals of our country. If the great middle class is forced to give up, what then?
I have read that so that the minister may-see there is at least something in the point that styles in houses and sizes of houses have had to do with the situation in the larger
cities. In the smaller towns and communities that is not so, but I noticed a few days ago in New York that large numbers of houses were marked "for sale."
