speechtext:
As the Minister of
Finance says, that condition is nowhere more apparent than in London, England. I point it out only because it indicates that there may be two sides to what seems to be a one-sided question. I confess that until such time as my mind had been set thinking along the line indicated by that communication, I would have wholly agreed with the view that there was room for large numbers of low priced buildings. But after reading that communication and setting my mind to think about some of the conditions to which my attention had been directed, I did not find it difficult to realize that there are two sides to this question.
With respect to highways, I think we should bear in mind that tourist trade in this country has become one of the most important if not our most important medium of securing moneys for the stabilization of our exchange. Last year, according to the figures presented to us, our tourist traffic amounted to more than our exports of gold. Every time a tourist tears off a ten dollar express order on New York, this means that a contribution of ten dollars has been made towards the stabilization of exchange, and every dollar that we spend which results in large tourist expenditures in this country does much not only to stabilize exchange but to give value to our dollars in other parts of the world as well as in the great republic to the south. But may I direct attention to the fact, referred to this afternoon, that in most places our roads are in an unsatisfactory condition. I know that steps have been taken to improve the situation at the entrances to our parks, and yet-I do not want to anticipate a discussion which must take place later-the truth is, because of the condition of our roads, that hundreds of people turned back last year at filling stations rather than come into Canada. They were told that the dust was such a nuisance that it would be inadvisable for them to go into our country, and they turned back and went somewhere else. I know that was so in some parts of our western country, and I believe that in one section of the maritime provinces the same was true, although to some extent it is being remedied.
With respect to the objection which was raised yesterday that we should not spend money upon provincial roads, I think there

Belief and Agricultural Distress.
was some misunderstanding on the part of the hon. member for Cariboo, or he would not have made the statement, because it was the settled policy of all governments since 1930 to assist the provinces in the construction of these very roads. The hard surfacing, for instance, of the road west of Winnipeg, for the purpose of enabling traffic to get to the parks without travelling through dust areas, was assisted by the federal government Right here I should like to make this observation with respect to the road between Rio Grande and Hansard. I had not known yesterday that the matter would come up in the committee and I had not the papers with me, but on looking it up I find the position to be this. There was no survey of this road. The minister asked me a question, as did the hon. member for Cariboo, and I indicated that I had no memory of a survey. I looked the matter up and there was no survey of the proposed road in this direction, but this is the position. What is known as the Northern Alberta Railways extend into the north country until they reach well up past Sexsmith and other points, Grande Prairie and various other small stations; and it was and is still believed, that from Rio Grande a road of 130 miles would take the settler down to Hansard without crossing the Fraser river but reaching that station on the Canadian National on the north side of the Fraser river, and thus he would be able to find an outlet to the coast with as little inconvenience as possible. I cannot think that the hon. member for Cariboo misunderstood me, for I would be the last man in the world to suggest that such a highway would be a solution of the transportation difficulties of that country. All it would do would be to provide a main highway from a point connecting with the Northern Alberta Railways at Rio Grande, which is not on the railway itself, but is a nearby station on the Northern Alberta Railways. When I say "nearby,' it is not as much as fifty miles; according to the figures I have it is under thirty, though possibly distances are measured in different ways in western Canada. At any rate, it is within reasonable distance of the Northern Alberta Railways. And the only point in the construction of the highway would be that it would travel west and south so as to connect with the Canadian National at Hansard station on the north side of the Fraser river. The communities having their small highways, not very good ones, would be able from the north to move south and connect with this highway, thus getting access to the coast.
That was the story which was put up by the settlers who desired this temporary solution of their difficulties. The hon. member for 51952-1604
Cariboo is quite right when he suggests that it would not offer a permanent solution of the transportation difficulty in the Peace River district. It would not, but it would be helpful in enabling the people of that area to find access to the coast through connection with the Canadian National railway at Hansard some 130 miles distant from Rio Grande. The hon. member for Cariboo overlooked one fact. Rio Grande is in Alberta and Hansard in British Columbia, and there has never been any question about our assisting interprovincial roads, because that has been done usually by the dominion itself with the cooperation of the two provinces for the purpose of providing what might be known as pioneer settlers' roads. That is all it would be in any event, and it would take the place of a railway for a little while at least, and enable these people to reach their markets through the Canadian National at Hansard without being driven back as they now are to Edmonton and the prairie country. In other words, they have no close rail connection that enables them to get out to the Pacific. As it stands now, that block of settlers who are settled north and east of Rio Grande have to find their way out on the Northern Alberta Railways to Edmonton instead of to the coast, which is nearer and through to which, they cannot hope under present economic conditions to secure a railway. I lend what support my voice can give to their request that they be given some little assistance for the purpose of enabling that road to be built as a joint enterprise on the part of three governments for the purpose of enabling them to get to the coast.
The other suggestions that have been made, it seems to me, resolve themselves into answering the difficulty to which attention was directed yesterday and to which my colleague beside me referred at length this afternoon.
I was called out of the chamber and did not hear the whole of his address, but it is clear that last year we had the appropriations before us and then the legislation at the same or at about the same time. Now we do not know what the appropriations are, and until such time as the appropriations are voted by this parliament the minister cannot do anything. This legislation does not enable him to do anything; it must be done under the appropriation. This only indicates that an appropriation is to be made and authorizes him to do certain things; but those certain things can be done only if he has the money, and he cannot get the money until the supplementary estimates are passed. That is the sequence of the movement of legislation,

Relief and Agricultural Distress
and as I said yesterday, I think we should have had before us, if it were possible, some idea of these appropriations, so that we might link appropriations and authority together and thus understand something of the picture.
It is not seemly that we should find the press and the populace engaging in guessing contests as to whether or not the government proposes to expend thirty or forty millions in a given way, when we know that until the appropriation is brought in they cannot spend a single sou. The minister at the present time has no authority to make payments of any kind because the appropriation of 1938 lapsed on March 31, and a new appropriation has not been made. Until such time as it is made, he has no financial authority to make payments, and so far as this bill is concerned it confers upon him only the right to do something with money when it is voted. But until such time as it is, this legislation is a dead letter and serves no useful purpose at all. It is therefore, I submit, important that we should have our appropriation measure before us at the earliest possible moment. I think it would have served to expedite the passage of this measure.

I should like to refer briefly to a number of points raised by the leader of the opposition, both before and after six o'clock. He made a number of statements before six o'clock, some of which I suggest that he himself will not regard with great satisfaction when he reads the report of what he said. The leader of the opposition spoke in somewhat contemptuous terms of what he described as the "academic mind."
I suggest to the right hon. gentleman that it is perhaps some vindication of the academic mind that since coming to this house I have never indulged in the kind of vicious partisan attacks of which he has been guilty on more than one occasion during the present session. I also say to him, and he will confirm it, that not since coming to this house have I ever raised the unemployment question in a manner which would emphasize its political aspects.
He has also, referred on more than one occasion to what he described as the scandal of patronage in the constituency of Kingston. I am going to speak of this matter moderately but in very definite terms. Two types of employment have been offered in the constituency of Kingston. On the one hand there have been temporary vacancies in the ordinary departmental services operating within that constituency. As a minister of the crown I have left the management of my constituency pretty largely in the hands of my local executive. In that respect I

believe I have not departed from a practice which has been followed in other years. I am not hypocritical enough to suggest that with respect to these temporary appointments, not under the control of the civil service commission, the executive have not nominated, and I in certain cases have not recommended, supporters of the present administration. The other type of work afforded in the constituency of Kingston has been under joint works programs with the provinces, to which my right hon. friend referred the other day. One type of work has been the restoration of Fort Henry in the neighbouring constituency of Frontenac-Addington. That work is done under agreement with the provincial government and in conjunction with that government, the dominion government contributing fifty per cent of the cost of that work. In the agreement there is a provision that in the employment so afforded there shall be no discrimination because of race, religion or political affiliation. I stated the other day, and I repeat now, that as far as that type of work is concerned I have given explicit instructions that this provision shall be observed and carried out. If it has not been carried out, I wish it to be distinctly understood that any departure from it has not been with my connivance, approval or consent. My right hon. friend has not hesitated from time to time to make these indefinite and reckless charges, regardless of the effect they may have upon the reputation of individual members of this,house. I hope he will accept what I have said as a statement of my position in relation to the employment afforded in the constituency of Kingston. I assure him that whenever I have had any complaint of any kind I have seen that such complaint was properly investigated, and I shall do so as long as I hold my present position as Minister of Labour.

Mr.Chairman, may I offer a few observations on the question which the house has had under consideration for the past few days. Honourable members have voiced criticisms and protests against the manner in which the moneys voted by this house have been expended in the various provinces. I may be permitted to take a few minutes to state what is being done in this regard in the province to which I have the honour to belong.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) stated from his place in this chamber that he would not allow the money voted by the House of Commons to his department for unemployment relief to be used for political purposes. I shall quote to the minister and to the house, without adding any comments of my own, cases where, in the province of Quebec, sums voted for unemployment relief have clearly been used for purely political purposes.
Last summer, I took the trouble to visit several parishes in my constituency, in order to ascertain whether the amounts granted to Quebec province were really being used for the purposes for which they had been voted. I should like to draw the attention of the house and particularly of the Minister of Labour to the manner in which the money voted by parliament was used in the parish of St. Benjamin. This parish received relief grants to which the dominion government contributed and I investigated among others, the case of a recipient of relief who had a wife and six children, several of which were old enough to help their father. One of the sons was 25 years of age; another, 23; another, 21 and another 17, all employed in lumber camps and earning wages sufficient to enable them to support themselves and to help their father. They were all living with their father in the same house. I could give the name of this man whose three eldest sons earned $780 during six months and who received at the same time unemployment relief during six months, from November to April. This man was the sole owner of his farm which, was clear of debt and equipped with rolling stock fully paid for. He had a horse, nine cows and other farm animals. His crop had consisted of 300 bushels of oats, 3,000 bales of hay, 100 bushels of potatoes and 400 pounds of maple sugar. He was therefore able to maintain his
IMr. Rogers.]
family. Moreover, he had three sons living with him who turned over to him the wages they earned in the lumber camps. In spite of that, he received unemployment relief. And I take upon myself the responsibility of stating that he received this relief solely because he was regarded by the inspector appointed by the government of the province of Quebec to supervise the distribution of unemployment relief in the parish in question as a friend of the party which is at present administering the affairs of Quebec province.
Here is a well-to-do farmer with an income sufficient to maintain his family, with three sons helping him and bringing him their wages, who receives relief allowances during six months, while another man, living in distressful circumstances, cannot obtain any relief. In the same parish, Mr. Chairman, a man with a wife and nine children, the eldest of whom is 16, has been refused relief. The provincial government inspector reported to the authorities charged with the administration of the funds voted by this parliament to Quebec province for the care of the indigent that this man has no need of unemployment relief. But see the difference! This man has only six cows-I am giving you the result of an investigation I made myself, I therefore know whereof I speak-he had harvested only 90 bushels of oats-you will recall that the other man had had a few hundred bushels-2,000 bales of hay and 50 bushels of potatoes, and he was living in a hut measuring 16 feet by 17. This family was undoubtedly in dire need. The local inspector saw all these things with his own eyes. He told me personally that he was acquainted with the situation of this farmer.
He even admitted, Mr. Chairman, that the man had a right to relief, and, after having denied him relief allowances during two months, he gave him a recommendation to that effect. However, when I went there in May, he had received nothing yet. He had a larger number of dependents than the other man, and he was destitute; and, yet, relief was denied him. Useless to say that he was not known as a supporter of the present government of the province. And that is the only reason,-no other can be seen,-why he was denied relief allowances, while such allowances were given during six months to the man who had no need of them.
I do not want to trespass on the time of the committee, but, as the minister has been good enough yesterday to ask all members to bring to his attention instances of political favouritism I was anxious to mention those few cases,

Relief and Agricultural Distress
but I may add others at a later time. I will acquaint him with what I have noticed myself in my constituency.
Mr. Chairman, as I was saying a moment ago, we hear complaints from other provinces. It would appear that in those provinces, provincial governments insist that their friends be put in charge of the administration of moneys and favours provided for the relief of the unemployed. As far as Quebec is concerned, I think no representative from that province in this chamber would contradict the following facts: For instance, the federal government contributes substantial amounts for the Trans-Canada highway project and for the construction of the Berthier-Trois Rivieres highway. I do not want to shock those on your left, Mr. Chairman, who have been objecting to political patronage in other provinces, but I want to acquaint them with the fact that for the reconstruction of that part of the Trans-Canada highway no tenders were invited. Instead, the provincial government just asked four of his staunch friends to quote prices and one of them got the contract.
It is a matter of common knowledge that a friend of the provincial government-I might ask the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Francceur) to confirm this, for the gentleman to whom I refer used to live in his constituency, and is now employed by the provincial government-has been entrusted with a. contract on a cost plus basis, the cost of which is partly borne by the federal government. In Carlesbourg and Beauport was not Mr. Frangois Nolin given work to do without tenders being called for, and at cost plus 10 per cent? The contractor stood no risk of losing anything.
Construction work on the Maniwaki-Senne-terre highway has been allotted to Mr. Hector Moore, without tenders being called for. Again, it is a matter of common knowledge that Mr. Moore lives in Maniwaki and that he is the brother-in-law of Mr. Auger, the member for the constituency of Gatineau in the Quebec legislative assembly. Patronage has been their sole concern. I am sorry to note that they would like to continue this same system, and I object to the further payment of moneys which, undoubtedly, are being used merely for political and patronage purposes
I could mention other instances. I need not refer to Mr. Hermann Barrette's gravel pit, for that is known all over the province of Quebec. Here we see one of Mr. Barrette's organizers buying for $400 something which is afterwards sold for $4,000 to the government, for use in connection with work
upon public roads to the building or repairing of which the federal government contributes an important share.
If I may be permitted, I also wish to bring to the attention of the minister, the persecution suffered by needy unemployed; a few instances of which I mentioned a moment ago, a persecution arising solely from political partisanry, and, as I say, no honourable member of this house will deny it, whatever party he may support. Things have come to such a pass that one is wondering whether he should continue to give his approval to the estimates whereby the minister wants us to put money at the disposal of the Quebec provincial government for so-called relief work. The minister has generously given his adhesion to the scheme of the Committee on the employment of Youth in the Province of Quebec. Again, I wish to bring to his attention this well established fact, that in all constituencies of the province of Quebec, not a single one, I think, of those who have been recommended by government supporters in this house to the provincial employment commission which was supposed to help these young people, has received the consideration he deserved, and it is also well known that in all constituencies those who were favoured had been recommended by local organizers or by candidates who were defeated at the last provincial election, or else by members who are on friendly terms with the Quebec provincial government. If any hon. member of this house can show me a single case where a young man he recommended was favoured by the provincial authorities, I will gladly admit that there is no political partisanship in the administration of the funds voted by the house for the youth of our province.
It was my privilege to take part in several by-elections since the present government came into power; in Bonaventure-the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) as well as several other hon. members who were there, could also tell you that voters in these various counties -were told in plain terms that if they voted for the candidate of the Ottawa government their names would be struck ofi the relief lists. I will point out to the minister specific cases that will prove definitely to him that such things happened in Bonaventure and Lotbiniere as well as in other counties.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to keep the house any longer on those questions, but I wish to point out that without a closer supervision of the funds voted by this house for

Relief and Agricultural Distress
relief in Quebec, the present government of that province will be left free to employ systematic persecution against certain groups of people on relief who are not sympathetic to that government.
Mr. Chairman, since we claim to have responsible government, since we from the province of Quebec are proud to think that our forefathers fought for responsible government, I ask the minister who is presently responsible for the administration of public funds if we can retain any longer the present system and) still claim to have responsible government.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise at this time to speak to one particular case, and no more. This afternoon the hon. member for St. Henry (Mr. Bonnier) took exception to certain remarks which had been made by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) with respect to works which had been promised during the by-election in St. Henry. A tunnel was promised under the Lachine canal at Cote St. Paul, which is the ward that gave an absolute majority to the hon. member for St. Henry out of the four wards in his constituency. The hon. member for St. Henry inferred that as the hon. member for Mount Royal was opposed to these projects, the other hon. members on this side who represented constituencies on the island of Montreal were also opposed. As far as I understood the remarks of the hon. member for Mount Royal, he said that the tunnel in Cote St. Paul, the abolition of a number of level crossings and the completion of the terminal station in Montreal, would involve millions of dollars. Those were election promises, and the inference has been that we are opposed to any projects for the alleviation of unemployment. That is a dangerous thing to have on Hansard as we are not opposed to any works provided they can be accomplished. However, we are opposed to promises and mathematical impossibilities.
The hon. member for St. Henry is not in his seat this evening. I want to say that he is a neighbour of mine and one of the most respected citizens of Montreal. He is an alderman for the ward that gave him the majority which has permitted him to sit in this house. The three other wards in his constituency voted against him. I am for the tunnel; the hon. member for Mount Royal is for the tunnel, as is the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) and the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. White). We are for the building of the terminal and the abolition of level crossings. The inference to be drawn from the remarks

in French this afternoon by the hon. member for St. Henry is that the members from the island of Montreal who sit on this side are against these projects. We are not against them; we are for them.
Two ministers of the crown-I do not know to what extent they are responsible-have sponsored a project near my constituency and I would be silly if I said I was against it. The hon. member for St. Henry must not forget that if Dame Rumour is correct, only 840,000,000 is to be provided for the construction of public works to relieve unemployment. If the promises made by the two ministers of the crown on a memorable occasion are fulfilled, there will be nothing left for the rest of Canada. My constituency is a bulwark for the constituency of the hon. member for St. Henry, at least for that ward in his constituency which gave him the necessary majority to be a member of this house. His remarks this afternoon were not correct as the other members from the island of Montreal are sympathetic with him. The hon. member has said that if these projects are not completed, the other four members from the island of Montreal should be blamed. I want it to be on Hansard that we are for his projects just as soon as they leave the field of imagination.
The Minister of Labour who is sponsoring this bill knows that the city of Verdun has done the best it could to carry out the provisions of the agreement under which certain works were constructed. We have acted according to specifications, or according to Hoyle, so to speak. Verdun is situated on the beautiful St. Lawrence river opposite the Lachine rapids, in the most picturesque spot on the island of Montreal. For twenty-two years the international highway to New York, via the lake St. Louis bridge and Malone, has been threatened with floods. During that time the city of Verdun has paid out $555,000 from its budget to protect this highway by increasing the height of the dyke. The dyke at this place is made of clay, whereas at other places, not so vulnerable, it is made of concrete. The employment commission has laid great stress upon the importance of the tourist traffic. WTe have been doing all we can to bring in tourists. They love to come to Verdun, the same as the Minister of Labour. When he came there he was received like a prince, and I believe he was satisfied with the work that had been done for the small amount of money which was provided, fifty-fifty, provincially and federally. With due respect to the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Tremblay) I give the minister all credit for what was done.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
Nevertheless, since 1906 we have had floods in Verdun. We have spent $550,000, though it was a federal proposition, due to the harbour works, the docks, and the Victoria bridge. In the thawing season ice banked up against the bridge, creating a reservoir by which the level of the water in the early spring was increased. We have endured this flooding. We have never asked for any compensation. Perhaps I should not say that we did not ask; we bothered the life out of the Minister of Public Works between 1930 and 1935, as the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart), who is now in his seat, will recollect. He went so far as to send engineers into our municipality to find out whether we were right or wrong. The reports are in the archives or the vaults of the Department of Public Works to the effect that Verdun needed a protection wall, for the protection of its population, for the protection of the city of Montreal, which was at the same level, and for the protection of Cote St. Paul, which gave a majority to the hon. member for St. Henry. We have protected them by our own finances. Now the hon. member for St. Henry comes along this afternoon and takes exception to certain words uttered by my colleague the hon. member for Mount Royal, who is not opposed to these works, but who, like the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. St. Pere), who is in his seat now, will not say where the wharves and the harbour are situate or where the cause of the danger and the threat against our city is located. They cannot say that we have opposed any of their projects; we have never done so, although the hon. member for St. Henry this afternoon indicated that we had.
I shall conclude my remarks by asking if, after all these sacrifices on the part of the city of Verdun, which has doubled its population in the last twenty years, which has a record in Canada-if I can be contradicted I shall be pleased to hear the facts-of having enlisted during the great war the largest number of men in proportion to population, which has made great sacrifices, and which can still balance its budget, our people should be punished because they have managed their affairs in a patriotic way. 'Let it be understood, Mr. Chairman, that we do not regret our sacrifices; but we say this, that the industrial centres must be taken care of, and ours is an industrial centre. We have done our best. We have controlled our population. Our population is made up fifty per cent of English from the other side of the ocean, good people, and fifty per cent French, also good people. They have been patriotic and should receive consideration. In the industrial centres, according to my experience, unemployment is worse than anywhere else. I hear of such projects as roads to be opened up from the Peace river. I hear of various reforestation schemes. But why throw our money in the bush? Why throw our money into rivers? Why expend our resources on places where the rivers can be used only with canoes to search for lost aviators? Why not take care of a population which, coming from the old country, has grown up with us, has benefited Canada and is willing to stay with us? If, as is rumoured, a sum amounting to $40,000,000 is to be spent, for heaven's sake let us spend it in places where sacrifices have been made for the upkeep of our civilization and the maintenance of our rights. I observe that the hon. member for St. Henry is on my side now.

The hon. member for Verdun, so far as I know, did not come out at the time to oppose these expenditures, so I have no doubt about his sincerity, and I am sure that the people of Montreal, especially the Liberals, will be very glad to hear the statement which has been made to-night.
As regards the objection voiced by the hon. member for Mount Royal, inasmuch as the hon. member is not in his seat at the
Relief and Agricultural Distress

moment I shall read from the Hansard report of the debate of February 8 last. On page 276 the hon. member for Mount Royal is reported as saying:
Is there anything of political significance in the increase in the amount of money required by the present government as shown by the estimates? Do they contemplate an election? Do they contemplate fulfilling some of the rash promises they made in Victoria, St. Henry, and other parts of the country? I would ask the hon. member for St. Henry to go through the estimates carefully. If he does so he will not find in them any reference to a tunnel under the Laehine canal; he will not find any reference to the removal of railway tracks from his division of St. Henry; he will not find any reference to an appropriation to be used to fill the hole on Dorchester street; nor will he find anything that will lead him to believe that the present government is going to build a bridge from the lower St. Henry division to the section of Notre Dame de Grace.
Knowing what took place during the election, is it to be wondered at that the hon. member for St. Henry took objection to this statement, no matter in how friendly a spirit it was made? I for one, notwithstanding my friendship for the hon. member for Mount Royal, have no hesitation in supporting the hon. member for St. Henry in his contention.
It was not my intention to speak on this particular occasion, but there is one item besides my answer to my friend the hon. member for Verdun which I think should come up. If I understood this afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps), he advocated having unemployment insurance whether the provinces agreed to it or not. As I understood his remarks-he is within hearing distance and can correct me if I am wrong-I think he said the government should take about the same position as was taken with reference to the Old Age Pensions Act, namely, pass an act and then let the provinces which are interested apply it. That may have looked wise at the time; but I feel that it should not be contemplated now, because I am convinced that it would lead to trouble. If this or any other government were to pass an unemployment insurance act against the will of one or more of the provinces, and proceeded to apply it to all the provinces which were in favour of it, leaving outside those provinces which were not in favour of it, I am afraid that those provinces which were left outside would make claims upon the government for compensation. I am sure that past governments were lucky to avoid situations of that sort under the Old Age Pensions Act, and I have no doubt that if the present government were to go ahead and put into effect an unemployment insurance act and carry it out in the

manner I have explained, there would be trouble. The hon. member for Winnipeg North suggested that a referendum be taken. There is merit in that suggestion, but I am afraid that it would land us in a good deal of trouble. Just as you find that provinces are unwilling to come under a general act, it might be found that certain sections of a province, or certain provinces, might express unwillingness through the referendum, and then what would the government do?

This afternoon the leader of the opposition referred, not unkindly, to the adulation which was showered upon the Minister of Labour in this debate, and which I am glad to say, did not come only from our partisans or satellites, as the hon. member for Mount Royal called us. The right hon. gentleman also said that in the days when he was in office there was no such kindness shown to those who were' then on the treasury benches. Perhaps there was not, and I am sorry. I can assure him that if my electors had seen fit to elect me five or six years earlier, I would have been one of the kind ones. But the fact was that there was then no reason for adulation because in the country everyone thought there was only one man in the government, and that was the Prime Minister, so that there was no need for compliments.
May I say that the electors of Jacques-Cartier are thankful to the government and to the Minister of Labour for what was carried out in the way of unemployment relief work in our constituency. We have been greatly benefited in Lachine and in other parts of the constituency. It may please my friends to my immediate left to know that in the matter of unemployment relief expenditures in my constituency I had no difficulty with the provincial administration. My secret was simple. I told my supporters, men of good will like myself, to go ahead and meet other organizations, not to look for trouble or to make trouble but to arrange things in the interests of the people of the constituency. That was the suggestion which I made to them and which they followed, and there was no trouble.' In that part of the constituency which lies in Montreal I did not have such good luck; but I hope that
with the experience gained in the last few months in Montreal, when the next works are carried out the results will be better.
The provincial government is at last going to build a highway for which I have been fighting so long in the house and outside. I desire to make but a very few observations in reply to what was stated by the Minister of Labour. In no sense did I wish to depreciate his academic training or his high record of scholarship; but where much is given, much is expected, and when he came to this house it was expected that at least his concern for democracy would be in keeping with one of his attainments. One of the curses of democracy to-day is political patronage in the manner in which it is administered in Canada at this very hour. If I made the observation that the conduct of the department indicated that the academic mind had brought nothing better to bear upon it than the untrained and unskilled mind, I but stated what is at this time the view of very many people in the country. The minister has said that he cannot personally be responsible for what takes place all over the country. I agree with what he says in that regard and on several occasions have so stated. But I would expect that when the Prime Minister of this country made the declaration he did the other evening, and when the Minister of Labour declared that he has followed those provisions of the agreements which provided that there should be no discrimination, some little effort would be made to see that this was done.
The minister selected a very bad illustration indeed. The Fort Henry work was done under contract, and the contract was let by the provincial government. It is all very well for the minister to say that he asked the provincial government that there should be no discrimination. But the contractor, the Frid Construction Company if I remember aright, had as one of its officers, according to the letterhead I have, the president of the Kingston Liberal association. And in answers to questions put upon the order paper, not

Relief and Agricultural Distress
one, two or three, but many of them, we have it indicated that men were given employment on the recommendation of that very man. Those were men who had no more claim upon employment than others unemployed. They were not selected by their names being taken out of a hat; they were not called; but this man sends a letter and on the strength of it we are told by the return filed in this house-not veiled insinuations of the leader of the opposition-that these men went down to Trenton and other places and were given their positions on the recommendation of that man.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister made it clear that there should not be discrimination, but we will leave it that they were not all on relief work. Fort Henry was a relief undertaking in part at any rate. But the statement of the minister is wholly beside the question. What does it boot that he should say to the government of Ontario; "There must be no discrimination"? The contractor who got the job has no such condition imposed on him. His job is to do the work, and he responded, as the return made in this house indicates, to the political necessities of the situation. The same thing is true in other parts of this country. Yesterday I mentioned Long Branch, and I might mention Banff. I might go all across the continent to Victoria. I might mention work in the provinces by the sea; there is the same sort of thing there. That is what is destroying confidence.
If the minister will look at the cost of administration, he will find that, according to the return, during the last fiscal year the cost of administration went up to S225,000, excluding the $17,000,000 disbursed by the agriculture department. That percentage is nearly twice, and sometimes much more than that, the percentage expended by the preceding administration. How is that accounted for? Why is it so? Would you not think something would have been learned with respect to it? This is not the time or place to take that up at length, as it will be taken up. But if we turn to the report made, it will be found

that the cost of administration is stated in the table in the report of the dominion unemployment relief commissioner, and it shows that on a total expenditure of $17,000,000 under the 1930 net the cost of administration was $43,000; the next year, with $42,000,000 expended, the cost of administration was $85,000; the next year the cost was $67,000 on a total of $26,000,000 in round figures; the next year, $87,000 on an expenditure of $41,000,000, or about two per cent. The next year on an expenditure of $40,500,000 the administration cost was $88,800. For 1935, on an expenditure of $49,500,000, the administration cost was $140,000. The next year, 1936, administration cost $179,000 for an expenditure of $47,000,000; and this last year, despite all the talk of economy, and all that has been said as to the desirability of exercising the utmost care with respect to our expenditures, $225,000 was spent for the administration of $27,000,000; or between eight and ten per cent, compared with two per cent in days gone by. Why is that? The answer is obvious. All one has to do is to read the reports in every part of this country, not one part only. The minister says, " I assure you I had nothing to do with regard to these particular matters." " Even in Kingston," he says, " I left it to someone else." I quite agree that he cannot be expected to deal with all these matters, but there are broad questions of policy for which he must answer. There are broad questions of administration for which he must be held responsible. That is one of them: The expenditure of $225,000 for administration cost on an expenditure of $27,000,000, relatively four times as much as spent by the preceding government for the administration of expenditures under their control. To talk about blank cheques and appropriation control having regard to a cost of from eight to ten per cent on the one hand and between two and three per cent on the other-well that is the position.
I asked the minister about camp No. 42 at Barriefield. It is not a question of an insinuation; there were statements in the public press and from the public platform as to what was realized for Bain wagons, horses and other articles which were in that storehouse which was burned. The minister says they have had the return to an inquiry with respect to that affair, about which I hope we shall learn something further presently. Those are facts, not my statements; they are in the returns brought down in answer to inquiries. Remember, we are few in number, scattered ail over the vast area of this county. We have been endeavouring to ascertain some facts. It has been a slow process to get at

Relief and Agricultural Distress
them. But the facts disclose, first, increased cost of administration, nearly four times as much as the former government expended on administration. Second, did members of this administration tell the people of Canada in 1935, when asking for their support, that they would not have a commission to deal with the matter but were going to deal with it in the same way as that which they had condemned? We remember the kind of speeches made by Mr. Peter Heenan in this house and others of that type, their condemnation of the government of that time for expending moneys, the charges made of political administration, and the holy attitude taken by the opposition of that day: Let us have power, we will see to it that this is conducted in a manner which will reflect credit upon our fairness, our impartiality, our desire to serve the body politic. That is what happened.
I think I hear the present Prime Minister, standing in this very place in the house, pointing out how sad it was that in this great country there was political administration of relief moneys; how desirable it was that we should have a great commission to coordinate and cooperate the work so that the provinces, the dominion and the municipalities might work together. One was almost moved to tears, hearing the pathetic tones in which the right hon. gentleman referred to what was taking place. Suppose he had gone out and told the electors of Kingston and other places that they had no intention of doing that; that all they intended was to appoint a commission to make some investigations, and then not adopt the commission's reports. Who will say that the report of the national employment commission is the final word they had to say about it? That is what we want to know. This commission that was to administer has not administered; the commission that was to deal with these matters has not dealt with them. There has been no change in administration, except to impose an administration four times more costly than we had before. That is what we have.
Then the minister referred, to expansion of trade and tried to assume or make it appear that I and other members on this side of the house were opposed to trade expansion. The trade agreement negotiated with the United States of America came into being because of proposals which had been made under the previous government and because every step that the law required in the United States had been taken before the present government came into office. The hearings before the tariff commission; the complaints; the opportunity for representatives of industry in the United States to present their case; all
this had been done before hon. gentlemen opposite ever saw office or heard of it. Why, sir, when the minister says we are opposed to the expansion of trade, only the other day we heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), with a couple of trade agreements, say, "Well, this is no change from the practice that exists to-day or from the practice that existed before we came into office. It is the same thing; only we have signed an agreement with them now, or the British consul did it for us down in some remote section of the world." The same thing may be said with respect to other countries, such as Australia and New Zealand, for example. It is true that the government varied the agreements they found when we left office, giving those two countries greater opportunities to sell their products here without any corresponding advantage to this country in those markets. It is true that there has been discussed the question of a new trade agreement with the United States which involves the motherland as well. But when the hon. gentleman says that this opposition has been opposed to the expansion of trade, he must know that the facts are entirely at variance with that statement.
I will tell you, Mr. Chairman, what we are opposed to. We are opposed to trade that renders it so easy for other countries to place their products in this land that they dispossess Canadian workmen from their jobs. That is what we are opposed to. We have lived long enough to see the Minister of Labour, who prepared a statement that has been thrust before the Rowell commission in every province in which it has sat, with the^ possible exception of Ontario-I do not know whether it has reached there or not- stand in his place and say, "Oh, do not do away with tariffs after all." And these compensating advantages, to which reference has been made, I suppose are nothing more or less than the statement made by the present leader of the opposition in the Walker theatre in Winnipeg in 1930 with respect to compensating adjustment; not compensating advantages but compensating adjustments.
Those are the facts. Trade? Of course, but trade on fair terms; trade that will not hand the Canadian market over to the stranger, to dispossess the Canadian workman of his job; trade, sir, that will do more, that will expand within our own markets, so as to provide additional employment for our own people. You may call it economic nationalism or anything you please; but there will be no solution of your unemployment problem in the cities and towns of Canada until, by

Reliej and Agricultural Distress
industrial expansion, every Canadian is afforded the opportunity to find a job in his own country. Let there be no doubt about that; whether it be an agricultural implement factory or a textile factory matters not.
When the minister talks about trade expansion, let him keep in mind one thing further. The conditions under which the emergency tariff of 1930 was passed were conditions the like of which this country had never before seen. What is more, it was the direct result of what had been done by the preceding government, following 1929, when the United States, as, the figures show, had entirely shut us out of their markets and left us the dumping place for their surplus products. We did put on an emergency tariff, and we saved this country from absolute insolvency and bankruptcy. What is more, the strongest testimony in that regard has been given not by Conservatives but by Liberals themselves, dispassionate, disinterested patriots who have looked about and seen the conditions, and who have realized that the steps which were taken, difficult though they were, had to be taken because of then existing conditions.
In connection with the sales tax we had the budget speech of the Minister of Finance a few short months before the election of 1930, cutting the sales tax in two in the face of a deficit amounting to millions of dollars, and imposing upon his successors the necessity of taking the steps they did take with respect to revenues. These are the facts with respect to that, and the sales tax has now risen to eight per cent, a figure never before reached and maintained in this country. I repeat, sir, that when the minister says those on this side of the house are opposed to the expansion of trade, he knows that is at least at variance with the record. Whatever else he may know, he can find from reading the records that his statement is at variance with the facts. What is more, the upward trend had begun long before this government took office. All one has to do is read the reports of the banks and financial institutions of the country; the upward movement had commenced and, what is more, the reduction in tariff imposts had also commenced. I sometimes wonder that any hon. member sitting on the other side of the house would have the hardihood to talk about tariffs in view of what followed after we imposed an exise tax of one per cent. That was condemned. We raised it to three per cent. I wonder if there is anybody in this chamber who read the debates or heard what was said who has forgotten the condemnation of that excise tax by the present Prime Minister. And it is
[Mr Bennett.]
still there at three per cent. We took it off Great Britain and empire products before we left office, in accordance with our promise that just as soon as economic conditions permitted we would make reductions. But that excise tax is still three per cent, sir, and the sales tax is eight per cent, two per cent higher than the highest it was under the late administration. The corporation tax is fifteen per cent. I think the income tax on individals has not been changed, but there are the facts.
I repeat that the expansion of trade is important; but the kind of trade that creates unemployment, that deprives Canadians of a limited market of only eleven million people, that makes us the dumping ground for the products of countries which deny us the opportunity of selling our goods in their markets, will not restore prosperity to this country.

If he will read the reports for January, February and March, he will have no difficulty in the world in finding out exactly what I mean.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the minister makes a clear distinction between relief and non-relief works. I have not in this house raised the question of appointments to casual vacancies, which right governments have exercised from time immemorial. I have made no complaint about that, and I have said in this house that I had no complaint to make in that regard.

No; that was with respect to what one might call the casual vacancies in the public service. For instance, I do not object to the Minister of Labour, if he finds it necessary to appoint a stenographer, to take some one who is friendly to his party. He has never heard me raise such a complaint But when it comes down to the question of public moneys that are to be utilized for the purpose of keeping people from being in the bread line and on relief, then I think it is clearly the duty of the government to see to it that men are not prejudiced by reason of their political belief.
If I say it has been done, I merely state what is known to me personally to be the

case in my own community. I can speak only with respect to personal knowledge concerning some few communities. For instance, in Victoria a man came to see me. It is true he may have been telling an untruth, but my investigation indicated that it was the truth. I certainly did know in Calgary how the Banff national park was operated, a matter we shall discuss when the estimates are taken up in committee of supply. I certainly know how other western communities have been treated. I have a large volume of correspondence about the matter which at the proper time will be made available. Whether or not I have been misinformed is another question altogether. But the statements have been made, and that at least I believed them to be warranted I believe goes without saying. I do not for a moment suggest that the minister can personally oversee all these matters, but I do say that a strong minister can see that it does not happen. All you have to do is to have it clearly understood by your officials that they will suffer the penalty of disobedience if they fail to carry out your orders.

That is a fair and proper question. I say to the minister at once that I believe there was an effort on the part of some people to use political means with respect to those matters. I know that at Calgary, where they were carrying on an undertaking in connection with the Currie barracks, I received a letter the other day from a man who is now no longer there, giving his experience as to the way in which men were taken on. The names were put in a hat and drawn out, regardless of what their political faith may have been, under the direction of the mayor. He said that when last spring he went up to try to get employment, it was no longer possible to get it unless you had a letter from a man called Hyde, who was my opponent in the recent election, or from Joe Shaw, who ran in Calgary East. He said, " I object to that. And, what is more, I have a solemn declaration I took with respect to some of these matters, because I felt they might be questioned."
What is true there is true with respect to some other sections of the country, because I have made inquiries in the same way. The minister is quite right when he says that in all parties at all times there are those who
will endeavour to do the very thing about which I complain. But the Prime Minister the other day declared his opposition to that. Frankly, I believe that if one takes sufficient time and makes it clearly understood to his officials what he intends to be the result of disobedience, he can accomplish his purpose. I say that to the minister.
I certainly do not expect the minister to run around and look at every John Smith and Peter Jones who may be employed, in order to ascertain whether or not he had a card or did not have a card, or whether he did or did not belong to this or that association. I believe the minister will credit me with not expecting him to do that. But I do say only one thing, something to which I had reference this afternoon-and I still stick to it-that it is one of the dangers which threatens this very democracy about which, in the language of one of our former members in another place, we talk a good deal about but which we are only bringing nearer to its own end by giving our approval to conditions such as these.
If you have a large part of the population who feel, as many of them do, that this is an unfair exercise of power, you create a condition which has an extremely injurious effect upon your institution. We are living in times which are very much different from the buoyant days of long ago. When I first came to this House of Commons in 1911, conditions were entirely different. I remained in it until 1917. when I was not again a candidate. I recall distinctly the circumstances under which, when war came, there had to be an entire change. It was no longer a question of war effort being limited to just one class of people. An effort made in that direction certainly brought about most difficult and dangerous consequences.
We are now fighting a greater war in one sense than we have ever been engaged in. It is a war against unemployment; it is a war against poverty; it is a war against conditions the like of which, despite our richness as a new country, we have never known before. I could not help thinking, as I am sure the minister must have been thinking this afternoon and this evening, of the promise made in Montreal by a minister of the crown when he said he spoke for the government, and when he gave a promise which is the exact negation of the present policy of the government. He said that the government would deal with the municipalities, if need be, despite what might be done by provincial and other organizations. That cannot but be injurious to the body politic. The question of promised public works projects stood in the same position.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
I suppose no hon. member has a wider academic knowledge of the historic side and setting of this situation than has the Minister of Labour. From what I know of his attainments I believe that is so. He must know that even with our limited knowledge, we know we are living under conditions which are tremendously different from any we have ever had before. The other day I was reading of what happened in this country in 1875. In that year there was a bread riot in Montreal. Alexander Mackenzie wrote a letter trying to still the agitation which existed regarding public works and matters of that kind, and saying that an engineer was looking into the situation. This happened, although a few months before Lord Dufferin had told the Canada Club in London that conditions were excellent. That was the condition in 1875. It was not anything approximating present conditions.
If I might be pardoned for saying so to the minister, I am greatly concerned about present conditions in this country. I am concerned because of the disharmony among the provinces. One finds it manifested in the briefs that have been presented to a commission which never should have existed, which has brought out differences on a scale never before known-a scale not expected- and never before manifested. We have here to-day a great and rich province making complaints about its contribution to the exchequer-and seriously, mark you. This is not as though it was some kind of spasmodic expression of opinion in a newspaper. It is a solemn and serious declaration by the first minister of the province, and by his responsible officials, in the greatest and most populous of our provinces. We have manifestations of disharmony and disunion in public statements in the other provinces.
It was that sort of thing which the present Prime Minister, when leader of the opposition, pointed out he desired to meet by appointing a commission for the purpose of dealing with this vast question of unemployment and relief. I was opposed to it because I felt we could not get a federal commission which would deal with it adequately. I believed we might be able to bring about through the provinces and the dominion a condition which would ensure some measure of harmony. Despite all that may be said, during a period of four or five years we brought the provinces together here year after year. The first suggestion of direct relief in Canada came from a representative of one of the two largest provinces. That is strange, but it is the fact. They felt that conditions were such that it had to be done and thev nressed

that it should be done. We said that we could not undertake this ourselves and we made them grants in aid. That was not the first or second year, as the minister will remember from the records. I realize, and I have never failed to realize; the late government realized that this was a very serious matter; that we were embarking on something which we believed would not last long. We said it was only a palliative. We believed that the upward trend would overtake the conditions which existed and we acted accordingly.
The minister knows that the improvement went up and up and up, and to-day there is a recession which was brought about in this country largely through what one might call the sympathetic feeling that has pervaded the whole world by reason of conditions which came into existence in the great country to the south. World trade, export trade, has diminished by hundreds of millions, according to the League of Nations. That is a great deal of money. That condition has been brought about through what one might call the impelling force of fear upon the minds of men who otherwise had vision and confidence and grasp and grip and the ability to deal with problems. The reaction in this country was later in setting in. We did not get the full force of it, and I am not sure that we have yet felt the full force of it. But we began to get it in the latter part of last year. It might be said that we began to feel its increasing weight somewhere about October. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) knows how it was reflected in the volume of exports and unfortunately in an increase with respect to some of our imports.
Look at the condition with respect to the cattle industry. We have been driven to sending our cattle across the Atlantic ocean to utilize a market which we have made just a market of convenience. We issued a warning that if this market were used' only as a market of convenience, you could not expect to have the facilities to send your cattle there when you needed them just because it was convenient. They cannot be sent into the United States. With the quota against us exhausted, we are trying to find a place across the ocean to which to send our cattle.
We might mention other matters. In my opinion that state of affairs necessitated a /ery bold course being taken at once by the government. Something is needed to restore the confidence of the people, to lift them out of the thought that they have to go through a depression just because our neighbours to

the south of us have to; that this 11,000,000 of people must necessarily suffer as 125.000,000 or 130,000,000 of people are suffering. I expected some action, but it has not been taken as yet.

As he pointed out, that condition was not entirely free from danger to those who were in the immediate vicinity. I pointed out that we did expect and we do expect and that this country expects some action. It is not good enough to say that we have repeated here what we did last year. I have, looked at the preamble and I shall discuss it at the proper time. There has been a little difference in the preamble each year. The mosaic has been differently shaped; the words have been cast about in much the same way as was done in the agreement of 1937 as compared with that of 1932. It was the same in the end, but the pieces were placed a little differently. The preamble to this bill is in that position.
May I say to the hon. gentleman I think he will find that something more heroic is demanded; not heroics, something more heroic. Something^ more striking is needed, something that will do a real job to restore a measure of confidence in the minds of the people, that will induce Canadians to rely more upon themselves, that will make them understand that the government is an instrumentality and not in itself an end, that the government which is here is here to help, that it is here not for the purpose of affording, shall I say, a living for all the population, but rather to assist the population in getting a living. I think it will be found that you must embark upon bold policies that are at variance with those which the bill now under consideration expresses, and this section in particular, contemplates.
